feedback: If a child gives 60+40=10, 70 or 700, show 6+4 and 60+40 with the same picture at two scales (counters then ten-rods) and name that six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100.
If a child says 35+50=40, slow down and count the tens being added: adding five tens to 35 gives 85, while adding five ones gives 40. Keep both comparisons visible side by side.
When a child derives correctly, ask 'how did you know that?' so the scaling or ones-bond reasoning is spoken, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Deriving a decade fact like 60+40 is scaling a known bond, not memorising a new fact: six tens plus four tens is ten tens = 100. A different move is using a bond inside a larger number — 35+5 uses the ones bond 5+5=10 to give 40. Which unit you add (ones vs tens) decides the result, so 35+5=40 and 35+50=85 are different.
learnerActions: Complete 6+4 on a ten-frame by sliding four counters in to fill all ten; confirm this is a known, secure bond making 10.
Switch the counters to tens: let each counter become a ten-rod (or restate each counter as 'one ten') so the same full frame now reads 100.
Say aloud what changed: 'six tens plus four tens is ten tens, which is 100' — the gesture and picture are identical, only the unit changed.
Repeat the tens-scaling with another known bond: 5+5=10 → 50+50=100 (five tens plus five tens is ten tens).
Separately, derive 35+5 by using the ones bond 5+5=10: 30 + (5+5) = 40, so here the 5 is added as five ones, not scaled to tens.
Deliberately contrast 35+5=40 with 35+50=85: in 35+50 you are adding five tens, not five ones, so the answers differ.
activities.title: Same bond, bigger units: scaling 6+4 to 60+40

feedback: If a child counts on fingers for 7+8 every time with no drop in effort on a second asking, do NOT impose timed drills or penalise finger use — keep practising the make-ten strategy and spaced recall without the clock.
For a derive prompt like '6+4=10, so 60+40=?', if a wrong value such as 10, 70 or 700 is chosen, return to the two-scale picture and re-establish six tens plus four tens = 100.
Ask 'which of those did you just know, and which did you have to work out?' to make the recall/calculation distinction visible to the learner.
activities.intendedInsight: Automaticity grows from secure strategy plus spaced, untimed retrieval; a fact becomes 'known' when recalling it needs noticeably less effort on later encounters.
learnerActions: Practise recalling facts to 20 in short, low-stakes sessions spread over days (e.g. 7+8, 15−8, 6+4, 9+4), rather than one long timed drill.
Mix in derive-a-fact prompts such as '6+4=10, so 60+40=?' and '5+5=10, so 35+5=?', choosing or writing the answer.
After each prompt, say which ones you just knew and which you had to work out.
Keep finger and make-ten strategy use welcome; the aim is that repeated facts need less effort each time, not beating a clock.
activities.title: Spaced, untimed retrieval to build automatic recall

feedback: Spoken back-and-forth gives retrieval practice but does not by itself build the make-ten strategy or the scaling insight; pair it with the ten-frame and two-scale work.
If a child cannot explain how they knew a fact, return to the relevant model (ten-frame or fact-family triangle) before more recall practice.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising recall and the reasoning behind it reinforces both the facts and the strategies (make-ten, inverse, scaling) that generate them.
learnerActions: Trade quick spoken recall prompts back and forth with a partner or adult (flashcard-style), e.g. one asks 7+8, then 15−8, then 6+4.
For each answer, the asker follows up with 'how did you know that?' — did you just know it, make ten, or use the inverse?
Keep it low-stakes and untimed; celebrate strategy explanations as much as correct answers.
activities.title: Playful recall talk: 'how did you know that?'
